content: Several techniques are available to achieve local anesthetic blockade of the brachial plexus, but it remains unclear which method is optimal for providing surgical anesthesia for the lower arm. The infraclavicular block (ICB) has been suggested to offer certain advantages over other approaches. To evaluate this, a systematic review was conducted comparing ICB to other brachial plexus blocks (BPBs). This review was initially published in 2010 and updated in 2013. The primary aim of the review was to assess the efficacy and safety of ICB compared to other BPBs for regional anesthesia during lower arm surgeries. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared ICB with other BPBs as the sole anesthetic technique. The primary outcome was the adequacy of surgical anesthesia within 30 minutes of block completion. Secondary outcomes included sensory block of individual nerves, tourniquet pain, onset time of sensory blockade, block performance time, pain associated with the block procedure, and complications. The search for relevant studies was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to June 2013. Conference proceedings and clinical trial registries were also reviewed. The original review included 15 studies with 1020 participants, while the updated review added seven new studies and excluded six, resulting in a total of 22 studies involving 1732 participants. The control interventions in the included studies were as follows: axillary block in 14 studies, supraclavicular block in six studies, mid-humeral block in two studies, and parascalene block in one study. One study compared ICB to both axillary and supraclavicular blocks. Nine studies utilized ultrasound-guided ICB. The risk of failed surgical anesthesia within 30 minutes of block completion was comparable between ICB and other BPBs (11.4% for ICB versus 12.9% for other BPBs; risk ratio [RR] 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.51 to 1.52, P = 0.64). However, patients undergoing ICB were less likely to experience tourniquet pain compared to those receiving other BPBs (11.9% versus 18.0%; RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.92, P = 0.02). Subgroup analyses based on the method of nerve localization and the type of control group intervention did not reveal significant differences in the risk of failed surgical anesthesia. However, when compared to a single-injection axillary block, ICB was more effective in achieving complete sensory block of the musculocutaneous nerve (RR for failure 0.46, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.60, P < 0.0001). ICB had a slightly longer onset time for sensory blockade compared to other techniques (mean difference [MD] 1.9 minutes, 95% CI 0.2 to 3.6, P = 0.03). However, ICB was faster to perform than multiple-injection axillary blocks (MD -2.7 minutes, 95% CI -3.4 to -2.0, P < 0.00001) and mid-humeral blocks (MD -4.8 minutes, 95% CI -6.0 to -3.6, P < 0.00001). In conclusion, ICB is as safe and effective as other BPBs, regardless of whether ultrasound or neurostimulation guidance is used. The advantages of ICB include a reduced likelihood of tourniquet pain during surgery, more reliable blockade of the musculocutaneous nerve compared to single-injection axillary blocks, and a significantly shorter block performance time compared to multi-injection axillary and mid-humeral blocks.
